Bonelab is a wildly ambitious VR title that pushes the boundaries of physics-based interaction in virtual reality. Developed by Stress Level Zero, it acts as a spiritual successor to Boneworks, expanding on its ideas with a mix of experimental levels, sandbox gameplay, and modding potential. Rather than focusing on a traditional narrative experience, Bonelab is more of a platform—a physics playground that encourages players to discover and shape the world around them.

The campaign, while present, feels more like a guided introduction to the game’s systems than a self-contained story. Each level presents a different theme, showcasing climbing mechanics, driving, puzzle-solving, and combat across various stylized environments. There's a surreal, almost dreamlike flow to the progression. The body-swapping mechanic, which lets you change your avatar's physical traits on the fly, adds a unique twist that’s tightly integrated into gameplay. However, the campaign can feel fragmented or unfocused, as its primary purpose is clearly to prepare players for the open-ended experiences that follow.

Where Bonelab truly shines is in its sandbox and community-driven content. The game offers a powerful physics engine that supports a massive range of interactions, from wielding medieval weapons to flinging enemies across rooms with makeshift contraptions. It thrives on emergent gameplay—moments that aren’t scripted but born from the systems interacting with each other in unpredictable ways. The inclusion of mod support from day one means the game evolves constantly, with the player community contributing everything from new levels and characters to completely custom game modes.

The VR implementation is solid but not without its challenges. Movement is fully physics-based, which makes for immersive, grounded gameplay but can also lead to awkward climbing or locomotion quirks. There’s a steep comfort curve; newcomers to VR may find some of the motion nausea-inducing, especially during high-speed sections or more chaotic environments. Still, for experienced VR users, the tradeoff is worth it—few games offer this level of tactile control and player expression.

Combat and traversal feel more refined than in Boneworks, but they’re still rough around the edges in places. Melee fights have a satisfying physicality, and gunplay is responsive and detailed, but some mechanics—like enemy AI and environmental interactions—can feel inconsistent. Fortunately, the game’s modular design and constant stream of user-generated content help smooth over these issues, providing fresh challenges and tools long after the campaign ends.

Bonelab is a game that knows exactly what it wants to be: an experimental, mod-friendly physics simulation wrapped in a VR framework. It’s not trying to compete with tightly scripted action games or deep RPGs. Instead, it hands the keys over to the player, saying, “Here’s a box of tools. Go break stuff.” While not for everyone—particularly those who crave structure or are sensitive to VR motion—it’s an outstanding example of what sandbox VR can look like when it fully commits to player agency. For fans of Boneworks, modders, and VR tinkerers, Bonelab is a chaotic, fascinating, and ever-evolving experience.

Bonelab has incredible graphics with my settings being at MSAA x8, SMAA on high, and HBAO at ultra with low bloom, low screen space reflections, low shadows, and low volumetric lighting as those seemed to offer much less visual fidelity and very minimal changes compared to maxing out anti aliasing. With these settings the game looks beautiful, crisp at any distance with no jaggies, and absolutely no stuttering or lag unless I’m loading a massive environment which then does not lag after loading. Even on low the shadows are pretty good with the volumetric lighting adding a large amount of atmosphere and the reflections being great. Overall the graphics and physics are miles better and I recommend the game simply for those reasons as well as the mods and sandbox.

Beat the game in 5 hours here's my review and opinion

Lets start with the basics and what i knew when going into the game
- Bonelabs is underwhelming compared to boneworks
- Bonelabs is more like a modding engine then a game
- Bonelabs has "the best" physics

Here's what i felt when i beat the game
- Campaign is alright its like people said underwhelming the campaign is mostly based off of minigames then a actual deep story.
The puzzles in the campaign i often accidentally skipped instead of completing them... Oops?

- The modding integration is kind of ass? It uses Mod.io i already dislike Mod.io for how it always crashes or spits out errors compared to Nexus mods and here it didn't even automatically log in compared to blade and sorcery and it didn't even allow browsing mods. Is that a luxury or something? To browse mods in game...

- The physics are honestly not that crazy for my feel i often even disliked it.
your character is fully physics based getting hit by a fast moving object in the chest will cause you to be flung by it which makes sense. HOWEVER my character would REFUSE to climb as he would be kicking the walls for no reason and i also managed to soft lock 5 times during my 5 hours. (Technically 7 but i managed to glitch out of the softlock) The reason why this happened was cause my hand somehow clipped into the wall and there is no way to reset it once that has happened apart from making it pick up a weapon while its going crazy

In general you could say this is a negative review.
And you WOULD be correct however the reason i am giving it a positive is mostly cause i lack knowledge of any actual good vr campaigns then anything else if i played a FUN and GOOD vr campaign then this would easily have been a negative

So here's the positives
The campaign allowed a decent variety of approaches. I often found a side route that i used to either get rewards or skip a part of the game which was funny in my opinion it felt like doing something unintended

The world has a nice vibe. 
I always liked watching boneworks and labs for its world, its got this hint of virtual reality X realism that makes it fun to watch and explore FOR ME atleast.

The death mechanic is cool! 
Sounds weird but i like the fact that you can be dying and still survive by killing a enemy just like in borderlands! Makes battles a bit more intense when everything slows down and you HAVE to kill a guy or you die.

Avatars with their own skills.
While in this game it was more of a gimmick then a actual "yeah we give you the tools figure out this puzzle goodluck" even the puzzles where you did have to swap it was plainly OBVIOUS what they wanted you todo so like. Eh... But apart from that its a cool CONCEPT, now to see it actually get utilized properly in a more interesting manner.

now the negatives.
The physics for me were Super wack. I don't know if i had something wrong but if a item would be on the ground i could not crouch and pick it up as my hand would move away from where i guess you could say my feet are and into where ever the void is. So i would have to avoid crouching physically and instead crouch using the joystick then walk back a bit and THEN grab the item like ??? You have a force grab but like cmon i just want to hold the items in a specific way while doing it with just one hand. And of course my hand would often clip through objects for reasons that i cannot explain as i still don't know how it happened

Controls were fucked too
I would get very off putting movement like getting stuck behind a wall and then launching forward
Very "ice like" movement i would slip and slide around. Holding a item would make it try to calculate how i grabbed the item through my hand position AND compare both hands which made a bunch of items like a bat break whenever i tried to swing it compared to swinging it with one hand. Also you always needed a start up with running in order to jump otherwise you would do the most pitiful jump known to man. Running is also confusing as its barely noticeable if you are running or not (That's probably a me issue though as i prefer physically swinging my arms in order to run in game then standing idle)
THOUGH after i played a bit i got used to all this so its just something you gotta get used to i suppose.

Now after ALL this i am not done with the game yet. As there is infact a port of boneworks for this specific game, and there's also a bunch of mods which make their own campaign that's the one advantage bonelabs has its a game about modding. So who knows what could be created given enough time

Don't be fooled by the puny amount of hours I have on this game. This is one of the best VR games that I have ever played and has ever hit the surface of VR. I don't know where I would be without the amount of inspiration I have gotten from this game and it's genre and how many hours I have sunk into the Quest version of the game. It has gotten to a point where I have bought this game two times, one on quest and now on PC + the BONELAB and BONEWORKS OST that is on sale for purchase. I own BONEWORKS aswell and I have to say that both games are really enjoyable as one is more lore focused which is BONEWORKS, it is like Half-Life while the other, BONELAB gives you infinite sandbox fun like Garry's Mod.

Without a doubt, this has to be one of the best sandbox games for VR that you'll ever find on the market currently. If you are looking for something more story-oriented then I suggest that you play BONEWORKS which is the prequel to BONELAB. If you like sandbox fun and playing with modded tools, avatars and other junk then this is THE place for you without a doubt. BONELAB may not be strong with it's campaign unlike BONEWORKS which was more lore heavy but BONELAB makes up for this by giving modders the tools to create their own levels, avatars and other stuff unlike BONEWORKS which didn't have proper tools for this.

This game has been being carried by mods for current past life cycle since it has released. You can play as any character from a fandom, or a game character, show or literally any media that is out their and I'm being dead serious. BONELAB for some people is seen as a watered down BONEWORKS (unfortunely people potray BONELAB as this game which has more quantity over quality) but I promise you this game has more meat inside of it with its mods and some people fail to understand this. BONELAB is a game meant to be modded, binded, molded into your hands. You are meant to have your own fun with the tools that the game gives you alongside it's almost endless mods that are already out their. It is a similar concept to Garrys Mod except you can do much more than you could on a simple 3D space with a mouse and keyboard.

The modders have been keeping this game alive for such a long while and I'm really not sure where this game would be if it was not mod-focused or didn't have it's mod creators. I have to say that these are some of the most dedicated modders that I've ever seen in such a large community. It caters to most of the people who are looking for mods with its large selection and theirs a point where theirs a fully fledged Multiplayer mod made by just one guy called "BONELAB Fusion" which I shamelessly spent far too long in, screwing off with friends and having a good time.

Oh and I guess theirs no other game where you can shove a knife up a guys rear while being Freddy from Five Nights at Freddys. But in all seriousness, this game is seriously worth your money and is NOT lackluster. Their's too many redeeming qualities for it to be called a "mediocure game" in my opinion and the lore is juicy, the gameplay is good and the mods are excellent.

Bonelab is to Boneworks what Garry's Mod is to Half-Life 2. Kind of.

It's a fun little side adventure in the VR-inside-of-VR world of MythOS with some interesting set pieces that are more adventurously designed compared to the levels of Boneworks. The remarkably short story feels more like an add-on to the sandbox, but forces itself to be front and centre for far too long before letting you play with all of the fun stuff. Kind of like being made to watch an hour long instructional video on how Steam works before you're allowed to open your library. It's not an offensively bad story by any means, but it went through one ear and out of the other the whole time I was playing.

Unfortunately, when compared to Garry's Mod's own mod support, Bonelab is far, very far, behind. Mods are handled through Mod.io - for the sake of compatibility with standalone headsets, and to simplify mod development as much as possible.

The ripcord, the iconic little character-model-changer device on your character's arm, is something that you can unfortunately only edit much later on - meaning you have to finish the entire campaign, which is a colossal PITA to play through if you only want to play with the sandbox and mods.

It's somehow the best VR sandbox while aggravatingly trying to not be just a VR sandbox.

My feelings on this are kinda complicated. On one hand, the basegame is deeply flawed. On the other, there's a fuckton of really good modded content.

To get the main grudge out of the way, the campaign sucks. Simultaneously far too short yet bloated to levels that would make Ubisoft blush. The big core selling point is also locked to like the final level of the game (home doesn't count, it's like three fights and sad music). Levels vary wildly and comically in quality and length, some are really damn fun while others end themselves in a few minutes tops. The good parts are the OST, the fact it only takes about four hours, and how easy it is to just download a dev-save or cheat mod and skip it all.

For positives, this is VR Gmod (even though Gmod has a VR-compatability mod, although it kinda sucks). Runs off Unity which is like fifteen geriatric shareholders and a repressed-homosexual puppyboy away from being open source at this point. Also helps that this game's running on some really potent shit, runs like a dream while holding one of the best physics engines in the business. All that means you get a lot of everything. R2 for codemods like Melonloader and Bonelib so stuff actually works, and Mod.io for your avatars, custom levels and gunporn. If it exists, there's probably a mod for it. Hell the side of the bodymall dares you to find a catgirl model. Main con is that the mod.io integration fucking sucks, a billion times easier and faster to just download the stuff and manually unzip and stick it in appdata (pro gamer tip: locallow).

Game also feels just plain fun to run. The way your avatar moves perfectly in-sync with your IRL body and how every joint and bone is factored in lead to a really immersive experience only comparable to this game's prequel. The bodymod and avatar system lets you make your own fun with challenge runs, seeing how far you can go as a fatass or twink in levels absolutely not built around either, the most fun I had in the campaign was propstacking and using a sledgehammer as a hook to get over a turntable as a morbidly obese furry. The way they pair with the marrow1 system makes every avatar feel distinct, having to learn your height and how you move and eventually figuring out how to control this new vessel just as well as the basic peasant you start with. There's also stat benefits, some avatars run faster or throw things further or can tank more hits, yet those usually come at the cost of size and unwieldiness, sure you may be ten feet tall and bulletproof but good luck reloading a handgun, sure you may be fast and a pain to hit but guns are a lot bigger than what you're used to.

In conclusion, this game's like a raw chicken breast. At base it's horrid and tough to stomach, but give it a nice sear and a lovely spice rub and it's now a five-star meal. Hell, a cabal of madmen ported over the entirety of Boneworks into this game, have your cake and eat it too.

Despite BONELAB being a VR game, it has quite frankly changed my life; modding is my main hobby and has led me down a path of a gamedev career that I would have NEVER thought about before. The game itself is great, it sets out to do what it intends; a VR title centered around modding and a campaign to demonstrate the capabilities of the 1Marrow interaction engine. Each "patch" contains improvements to Marrow, and incremental improvements to the campaign. Don't think of BONELAB as a campaign with modding support tacked on; this is a VR modding platform, driven by 1Marrow, demonstrated in the campaign.

The raw value a user gets out of this game should not be determined by the campaign, which many perceive as too short. Rather, it should be determined by the value from mods, and the campaign as a side value. The MarrowSDK is still relatively basic, at the writing of this review we still only have official support for levels and avatars. However, the advent of the community contributed to and created by, Extended SDK, allows for spawnables and complex mods in general to be made. People say that the MarrowSDK is "holding back the mods", however most modders utilize the Extended SDK, making this "limit" people say is hindering the game, not be an issue. 

As a modder myself, I am FULLY satisfied the the game as a whole, the SDK and Extended SDK capabilities, and community.    I have NEVER had to limit my scope of a project because of a limitation; I've been able to accomplish what I set out to make, could be a map, gun, avatar with abilities, etc. The strongest aspect of BONELAB mod creation and development is the community; a strong, resourceful, and inviting community willing to embrace and help create. Starting in late 2022, I've amassed over 1.2 million downloads across all my mods. If that doesn't show the success and value people hold of this title, then I don't know what does. If you think this game is "dead" and people don't care about it anymore; you are greatly mistaken; just take a look at the download count of some of the most downloaded mods.

Purchase this game if you value the hard work of modders, the fun of mods and a campaign, and the hard work Stress Level Zero and their dedicated team have put into Marrow. To date, it is the has the most sophisticated VR player rig in any VR title so far; and with indirect progress being made towards future titles via Marrow being the backend of them, it will only, and always get better from here.

I ramble so my subjects may jump all over the place. I tried this game a year ago. It felt awful then for multiple reasons. Now. It feels better... but still not good.

Boneworks was better in almost every way. Guns felt better, movement felt better, physics felt better, and it didn't make me motion sick. There were not an extreme number of instances where you could fall easily in Boneworks. Here in Bonelab falling seems to be a necessity and almost encouraged to get motion sickness with how many places i can fall extreme distances or the player character gets moved out of the player's control, like entering a minigame area. The "improved physics" feels like all they did was buff the player strength. That's it. It CAN feel more responsive, but almost everything now feels weightless. Sure its fun to grab objects and kinda chuck em around, but honestly feels less interactive to me. Two handing my pistol felt wrong because it'd cause it to weirdly wave around upon grabbing so aiming was off till it corrected out of my control. And then one handing a pistol well apparently our arms are made of noodles because I found it hilariously floppy when trying to aim one handed. Guns like pistols feel like toys now with the little movement they have when racking them. I'm not saying it needs to be the dramatic kick back when racking it like Boneworks, but it was satisfying to do that. Also my biggest complaint, which is also my goofiest, comes from trying the parkour. I was trying to look down by my feet to make certain jumps or descents, and I couldn't, because there was an annoying pair of virtual breasts in the way making it so I couldn't really see below me at all. I walked off edges several times because of this. I will happily go play Boneworks for a more immersive physics based experience where things had weight, guns felt good, and there aren't breasts blocking me from making more precise jumps and climbs

The controls feel weird and unresponsive, which is only made worse by poor performance. Sure, you can grab things wherever you want- so long as "wherever you want" doesn't include the literal only way you would hold it. Add that to the utterly bizarre proportions of much of the melee weapons, and it just feels gross. If you want to shoot guns, play H3VR, and if you want to hit things, play BnS. This game only fails at both.

What a fall for a studio that has been truly brilliant until now. The basic concept of the game is good and has some really appealing ideas, nothing less is expected from Stress Level Zero after all... but the execution... this time it didn't cut it for me.

The storytelling is quite disjointed, and although I didn't get very far into the main story, I had a constant sense of emptiness that would have been ignorable if it weren't for the technical aspects of the game (spoiler alert): it switches from moments of "rail-shooting" (literally sitting in a mining cart shooting fixed targets like an amusement park), to first-person go-kart tracks with a steering wheel that is so sensitive that it gave me motion sickness even though I am extremely used to VR, don't suffer from motion sickness, and have played numerous VR simulators of various types, including flight sims), to what was really the last straw for me: some sequences where you change "avatars" and find yourself in bodies that have proportions different from the human body, particularly in the length of the limbs, which makes even interacting with simple objects extremely strange, not to mention sheathing weapons and objects, which is already more complicated than in many other titles due to how the object anchor points have been calibrated.

I also found the movement and parkour much more "awkward", and I don't particularly like the fact that essentially every "level" is a timed course that is supposed to encourage you to climb the leaderboards.

I'm sorry but this time it didn't work for me, there are now much better titles out there and if you really want to do something in VR, I'll tell you: replay BoneWorks or jump into IntoTheRadius, personally I feel that depending on what you're looking for, you'll benefit in both cases.

[i]
I waited a long time for a sale to finally try this title, as I have loved the first game (Boneworks). Now, after completing the "tutorial"/intro and some gun courses I am absolutely devasted. Maybe it was nostalgia, or I am simply just used to better games at this point but it felt worse than the first one. 
Now for why: [/i]

[h1]STORY[/h1]
The story felt like a mixup between the first setting and a generic "oh no escape this vr hell"/isekai whateverthef*
 with lore on text scattered! about the place. In 30 minutes of playing this physics sandbox I approx. read 15 minutes of random flavor-text. The texts itself were cool and you could try to imagine the settings or things behind everything IT WAS JUST SO MANY BREAKS OF READING. 
Okay, mechanics learned - read 2-5 tablets of text.
Alright, enemies introduced - read another 4 tablets before the next room/area.
Oh look, a secret - who could have guessed - some more reading.

An argument can be made here "Just skip it" - yes, I had to, against my own preference of using VR to immerse myself and to experience the art and worlds developers create within games.

[h1]GRAPHICS[/h1]
The graphics were okay - due to the "virtual reality" world some simpler sci-fi effects can be overlooked the rest was medium level. Most textures were clear enough to read all the stuff on it, which is great, but many parts of the geometry were 2d textures instead anything geometric you could touch. 

[h1]SOUND[/h1]
The sound design was good, impact sounds and guns felt or sounded heavy and impactful, music was nice and the va stuff for the story sounded fitting aswell. The spatial audio was 50/50, everything sounded exactly as you would expect depending on your surrounding. But to try to orientate yourself on sounds was more than weird. In between areas there were very abrupt changes, sometimes objects made sounds from places you could not find or where they should not have been, that kinda pulls it back a bit.

[h1]PHYSICS[/h1]
This game/franchise focused itself on its physics engine, I even followed multiple dev-blogs during its development and was fascinated. And it's good! The only gripe I have and now recalled for the first one was your own interaction with it. 
If you set things in motion they behave how they should, you can smash stuff, hook things, throw or tip them all great - BUT: You fight against the game and controls to get them into motion in the first place. 
It's not that its just explained that some things with more weight need 2 hands, its so heavy it is nearly impossible to do otherwise. Everything seems to lag behind and strictly and maybe phanatically follow newtons first law of motion (and maybe more so for the resting state).

This and the way you grab your guns (with fairly simple interactions) makes your own "vr-body" very loose and feel disconnected from you. You can grab everything thats designed to be grabbed, but nothing else. 
Climbing anything other than yellow painted story pipes-for-climbing is impossible and discouraged. My headset was positioned in a way that was 15cm behind my neck, when i turned to look down, it stayed in place even when bowing forwards and when fighting with something else than a "melee weapon" - A broom i found in a "secret" room - i fought the broom moreso than the enemy. I lost my second hand grip with every swing and if I even hit the little enemy from the first game, instead of a hefty whack and instant kill (like with every other weapon, even 1 handed) it just felt like a squeeky toy...
[hr][/hr]
[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]
All these things combined just let me realize "damn... I don't even want to play this, I'd rather play any of the major vr games that specialized itself in one single thing"

[i]Meaning.... there are some games which were released even earlier or developed for longer that do the things they advertise very nice! Medievil fighting games with weapons and great bots that make you feel like an adventurer, berserker or knight - delicious weapon simulations with insane precision, handling and graphics - or great and immersive story focused games. [/i]

They be like the most mindless zombies ye ever did see – no different shapes, no fierce designs, just a bunch of landlubbers shufflin' towards ye. And what's worse? In a physics sandbox, I be expectin' a dance of blades and mayhem, not this mind-numbin' swatting of flies.

Now, the tale, or lack of it, be another grievance. Elden Ring tosses ye into the thick of it, and it works like a charm. But with Bonelab, it be more like a sudden plunge into the icy depths with no warnin'. No narrative to pull ye in, no warm-up to get ye blood pumpin'. Aye, playin' with the physics be a joy at first. Smashin' things, experimentin' with the elements – a true pirate's delight. But before ye know it, ye be askin' yerself, "What now?" The novelty be wearin' thin, and there be no buried treasure to keep ye huntin' for more.

In the least acrimonious way possible, Bonelab is a mostly disappointing title. The story mode is nowhere near as mysterious, fun or engaging as the original Boneworks, Finishing this game felt more like a relief than anything else, and it's a very anti climactic ending, I'm not sure if it can be called anti climactic, as the build-up to the end of the game was more or less just waiting to see the end screen because you're so tired of playing it, 

The main gimmick of Boneworks was the physics, and all of the physics based puzzles were satisfying although scarce throughout the game, as they do get repetitive and annoying, 

Bonelab is a game that annoys you and frustrates you a LOT, and discourages you from finishing the game. Physics is a very important feature, but it also needs to be satisfying and fluid, and the environments and puzzles greatly facilitate the satisfying feeling of the physics, which Bonelab unfortunately fails at in my regard. The puzzles and level design are just not there, and it makes everything feel needlessly difficult. It just feels broken and everything never works on your first try.

In terms of what the game does right, the combat feels satisfying especially when you're playing as a more heavy character, but it still suffers from the same clumsiness as the rest of the physics, especially with all of the handling of shotguns, The rest of the weapons, especially pistols, feel great and have great feedback. The combat is certainly a highlight of this game which is not used enough, especially in the latter half of the game (the part which feels like a chore to complete)

In my personal opinion, if you're here for the story, play Boneworks. If you're here for the mods, consider buying it, but keep in mind Boneworks might still be more fun. Definitely don't buy this game first either way

First of all, this is a intermediate review and does not represent the full game nor will it be representative for all users - it's a very specific hardware set which I can write this review for, it's not for everyone.

Second of all, Boneworks is for me - together with Half-Life:Alyx - what I would describe as AAA VR title (quality/gameplay-wise). I won't go into detail why, but it will be obvious to everyone when looking at gameplay of it. Everything is physics-based, everything can be touched, there is a "free" way of interacting with stuff, everything has weight, etc. Most other VR titles are what you would call "point and click" compared to fully fledged which is great!

Sadly, playing this on a Pimax 5K Super and Index Controllers comes with a lot of caveats for this game (which weren't a problem in Boneworks):
- Native Pimax via SteamVR won't even load the menu (it just blackscreens)
- The work around does sort of work, but I didn't remember my Pimax to be that bad in blacks (might be a Pimax XR thing, which is necessary to play at all)
- The work around (and sort of without it as well as far as I've heard) requires Index Controller to Oculus Controller emulation. Those don't have 5 fingers, not even speaking about spatial tracking of them and thus feels very digital compared to an "analog" experience with native Index Controllers.

What I have seen so far apart from my mostly hardware issues is that the physics feel a bit clunkier (mostly talking about hitting stuff and clipping into them; although there were also cases which felt A LOT better than Boneworks), can't really pin-point what it is tbh, but it's not a big deal with what this game seems to offer. Big respects to making VR more inclusive with the Quest-support but since this also requires a common base for input, this seems to hurt the PC version at least a bit.

It really hurts after those fun times in Boneworks and all the love I put forwards to Bonelab to not recommend this. But as said, this isn't the experience for everyone, but Pimax and Index and should not represent the general state of the game which is still years ahead of most other VR games, it's a league of its own. I'm hoping big time for a patch to fix those issues, which would definitely switch this review to a positive one, no doubt. Still love you SLZ, but please enable the potential of the game for guys with special hardware like me as well again <3

Before I even review the game, I'd like to say I believe this could have been a really cool DLC of Boneworks. I believe this didn't need to be it's own game and could have just made an update to Boneworks. This game is literally an improved version of Boneworks, nothing really life changing. VERY little is really new about the game. Sure, there's some new gimmics, but it's the same game.

First off, I've played 179 hours of Boneworks as of typing this review. I'd play it mainly for the arena mode. I'd put on my favorite music, and just vibe. Sure, there'd be some slowdown, there are days I wish they'd fix some things, but it works.

As for this game, they broke a lot of what I enjoyed about Boneworks. The gun play is broken, guns don't like to stay in one place and move on their own, and the horrendous addition of forced virtual stock. Yes, there's a virtual stock, no you can't turn it off. Some times it works great, reloading the shotgun SOME TIMES feels good. Other times I look down and the weapon I'm holding is completely upside down. Tracking seems to break more often in this game than any other, I genuinely thought it was my headset, but I tried this game on another headset and had the same issues.

Things I actually liked so far:
- Arena mode is looking good, but you run out of ammo VERY quickly. There's only a VERY small amount of new weapons in the game, so not much changed since Boneworks. I very much look forward to custom arena areas.
- FPS remains pretty steady, not as much lag as the first game.

Biggest issues:
- Guns don't work like they should: As mentioned above, guns would randomly shake and pop out of your hands, turn upside down, or you just can't grip them. As someone with nearly 200 hours in Boneworks, I know how the game works and it's genuinely annoying.
- Forced virtual weapon stock: For those who don't know what it is, it's game mechanic that mimics the way you would put the stock of a gun to your shoulder. 99% of ALL games allow you to toggle this on and off, but this game has no option to turn it off, so guns with stocks will feel VERY different than they should.
- I don't care what anyone in the forums say, starting your VR game with the player literally hanging themselves is NOT a selling point and isn't going to help with sales. I have no earthly idea why this is a forced LITERALLY the FIRST thing you do in the game. My advice is to just have a platform in front of the player, they step on it and they are transported to that exact same scene but their arms and legs are bound to something while it's set on fire. GOING THROUGH THE ACTUAL PROCESS OF HANGING YOURSELF ISN'T NEEDED OR ASKED FOR IN VR.

Until they update all the issues others and myself have outlined about the game, I cannot recommend this yet. Stick with Boneworks. For now, I'll leave this review as it is.

The game's narrative is hollow and the game/level design is not intuitive. Once you get to the lab after a half hour, you just get dropped in and are left to figure it out for the most part. Just give the player a HUD and tell them what the fuck they're supposed to do, maybe even a health bar instead of shitty vignette that you can hardly see. 

That being said, it has the best physics engine in VR so if you want to see an example of the most advanced game in the space other than HL:Alyx, then Bonelabs has it. However, what made Alyx so compelling is a good narrative and level design so its not impossible to get started and you're not trying to master the physics and figure out what the fuck you're supposed to do to advance the game at the same time. That coupled with the fact that playing VR for more than half an hour makes most people sick leaves this game falling flat on its face as just challenging and annoying. 

They made this game for people who play Boneworks all the time instead of taking the opportunity to bring new players into the space and hold their hands to show them the true capabilities of VR. Instead it's a game designed for VR "Experts" that left a bad taste in my mouth and after about an hour it becomes frustrating and exhausting. Hopefully the modding scene makes this game more palatable in the future but for now I'm hard-pressed to recommend this to anyone who doesn't play VR games all the time.

As a huge fan of the first game (it's one of my favorite VR games), I gotta say... This game really doesn't live up to the first and in many ways feels like a downgrade.

For starters, let's talk about the engine. I know Boneworks has a reputation for being janky but this game seems just slightly worse in this regard than the first one. Half the time when you go to grab a mag, you will pull out your belt item, or grab nothing. Shotgun pumps work maybe 50% of the time. When you grab certain guns, your hands will sometimes freak out and spaz all over the place (try grabbing the AK on the front and you'll see what I mean). The worst of all is sometimes you'll just get completely stuck in geometry and have to restart the level. It's annoying and maybe I have "rose tinted glasses" for the first game but I don't ever remember it being as janky as it is here. Hopefully it can be fleshed out with future patches but as for right now, it doesn't really work that well.

In terms of the story, well... There isn't really one, or if there is, its a complete cluster(expletive). You have basically a tutorial showing you how the different player models work (will get into that later), then you have a few minigames and then 1-2 missions to finish it off. If there was a story, then it completely flew over my head. It just feels like a bunch of disjointed missions and then it ends. Granted, the story in the first game wasn't mindblowing or anything like that but it was leaps and bounds better than whatever this is. Also, I ran into multiple bugs that required me to restart the level to pass. Stuff like doors getting stuck, my hands and legs getting stuck in geometry, stuff like that. [spoiler] Also, there's a part in level 13 where you're in a tunnel, and you have to use launch pads to catapult yourself through the tunnel. This barely worked for me, and it took like 10 minutes to finally get it to work and not bug out [/spoiler] Honestly, if you are going to buy this for the custom content, I wouldn't waste your time with the meager story offerings here. Just download a 100% save and spare yourself the time and headaches.

You can now drive vehicles around. Sounds great on paper but in practice these are literal headache/stomachache machines. I've never once gotten sick while playing VR (aside from the first few times I've played it) and I legit had to take breaks every lap I did on the karting level. I very much doubt you will use any vehicle ever again after trying it and being nauseated by it the first time.

You can also now easily switch out your player model, and these player models all have different traits that you have to use to complete the story. Let's go over each of them:
- Strong: Probably the only one that actually feels right. Like the base character but can roll bigger boulders/pick up heavier stuff more easily.
- Fast: Honestly doesn't really feel much different to the base character model. I hardly even notice a speed difference.
- Heavy: His body takes up way too much of the FOV and his tutorial mission revolves around melee combat, which feels awful in this game (TBF it is also pretty bad in the first game)
- Small: Kind of pointless honestly. There's like one part of the game he's actually useful, and that part isn't even in his tutorial level.
- Light: Again, pretty much feels almost exactly the same as the base character model.
- Tall: Probably the worst in terms of jankiness, and also has the absolute worst mission in the game as his tutorial.
It is kinda neat that it's really easy to switch between all your player models.

In terms of modding, yes it's way easier than the first game. But, the problem is that the first game already had a solid base game underneath. It didn't rely on community made content to be great. This feels like the opposite of that. You pretty much have to put mods in to get your money's worth. Also, it begs the question: why didn't they just implement these modding tools into the original game?

The new guns are a plus. More variety is always welcome.

Disappointed enough to write a review. I had loved Boneworks so I was really excited for more of the same formula, but after completing the main content of Bonelab, I'm frustrated by all the downgrades and missed opportunities. Some folks may play Bonelab having never experienced Boneworks, and that's fine, but I don't think it unfair to compare a sequel to its predecessor. In short, Bonelab is simply worse than Boneworks in every way, perhaps except for the mod support, but I'm not sure I'll stick with it long enough to appreciate that aspect of it. 

Some thoughts, in no particular order, and some items more major than others:

- Graphical fidelity and performance take a hit. Every level has a bit of a haze to it, and there are scintillating artifacts and aliasing at each level of graphics quality. For me, even the "Performance" setting runs more poorly than Boneworks at high settings.
- Levels are all much smaller with seemingly less variety. Some levels feel more like fanmade, demo worlds rather than fully fleshed out experiences.
- Others have rightfully complained about Pillar Climb, but it was the mine cart level that had me scratching my head. Maybe enemies were intended to be riding the carts that pull up alongside you on parallel tracks but they were removed for performance reasons? Unclear. But the level feels somewhat aimless with just the single track and wooden targets. Other levels leave one similarly thinking "oh, that was it?" with some regularity. Any physics-based puzzles are obvious and more a chore than a challenge.
- Flipped the go kart on the last lap of that level. Avatar wasn't strong enough to flip it back over. Had to finish the level by jogging the rest of the lap. Wild.
- The opening scene is certainly a choice. I don't know how it made it to the final cut without someone questioning whether it was a good idea or not. A warning and/or opportunity to skip would have been great.
- AI is unimproved. Enemies will often rush you at the start of a firefight, you'll defeat them all easily, and then you'll have a quiet walk to the end of the level unbothered. Take this time to think about why you're bothering with it all.
- Your hands are offset somewhat from where they are in real life. You get used to it, sure, but it seems like a very basic thing to try to get right. So many other games have no trouble with this, including Boneworks.
- Enemy models are simplified. Nullbodies comically so. I haven't counted to compare, but it feels like there are fewer enemy types even if there are more models for enemies that behave the same way.  
- I played with Index controllers and some strange choices were made in how they behave compared to Boneworks. You can no longer grip an item with just the palm grips, you must also touch the trigger slightly for it to register as grabbing the item. Of course, in the heat of things, you may over-commit to the trigger touch and fire a round when just picking up a gun.
- Playing through the main story, whenever you transition to a new level, all of your weapons will reinitialize unloaded. This is a minor gripe, but it seems like a strange choice. Often I'd forget to reload any weapon but my primary, and in a firefight I'd pull a secondary weapon to find it unloaded. 
- The avatar system is interesting, if gimmicky. But, not enough was done in the level design to really justify it.
- It feels a bit cheap to complain about the narrative in this franchise so I won't linger, but it's bad. Boneworks's plot was loose at best and get progressively worse, but Bonelab's is somehow a further step down. 
- Pulling yourself up onto a ledge was tricky in Boneworks but you felt a bit of pride once you got the hang of it. In Bonelab, it's again somehow more difficult. Be prepared to yeet yourself backwards into the void a few dozen times just trying to climb onto a wall. A good amount of the challenge to Bonelab is in fighting the engine to do simple things.
- Overall, it feels a bit like Bonelab is banking too much on the promise of user-generated content. One can't shake the feeling that maybe its flaws were brought up in development but perhaps dismissed because "players find jank charming!" or "modders will run with the ideas!"

Bottom line, just play Boneworks. I've gone back to it to cleanse my palate and it's maddening how much more polished it feels. A stranger to the franchise would be justified in assuming Bonelab was the original and Boneworks the new and improved sequel.

To my surprise, after finishing the campaign, I got something that felt hollow, disjointed, and completely lacking in presentation and polish.  Graphics-wise, it doesn't seem better than the original.  BoneWorks, to my recollection, had some pretty good set-pieces, and most of the stages had at least some sort of lighting/details in it that made it distinct from each stage.  

With BoneLab, it feels like a collection of stages strung together, with only the most bare bones amount of effort put in the graphics and presentation.  Most stages feature flat, dull lighting and blocky meshes with some very basic texture-mapping.  Hell, I don't think many of the models even use normal-mapping (or at least the flat lighting is causing me to think that).  In addition, most stages felt claustrophobic and very corridor like.  I remember the original BoneWorks having plenty of wide-open spaces to roam around.  

Worse, there doesn't seem to be any new assets in the game.  Nearly every enemy I can recall running into, feels exactly like previous ones in BoneWorks.  As a matter of fact, I think SLZ re-used the same meshes, or downgraded the detail on them.  

Lastly, the single-player campaign didn't have a sense of coherency or overall narrative ark.  There doesn't seem to be any momentum or build-up to a final event, or anything interesting to encounter.  As I mentioned, most stages are corridors and flat, low-texture-mapped walls.  It feels like someone built a basic UT4 game but forgot to add the assets in.  If this was intentional, I don't remember the first game ever being this bad.  Other then that, the plot was completely un-memorable and after I finished it I thought 'that's it'?

Again, I am just coming  from the perspective of someone who liked the first BoneWorks and it's single-layer campaign.  I wasn't interested in this game for the lulz or the mods.  I just wanted a good experience for my $40, but instead it felt like I overpaid by about $35.  I don't know what Stress Level Zero was thinking when they cooked up this sequel and its story.  It really feels unpolished and that lack of effort was put in to rush it out as quickly as possible.  It almost feels like a cash grab.

I liked Boneworks so I was hyped for this, but it is just an empty shell. It has virtually no content. The devs depend on user generated content for their 40€ game but apparently not even that is really a thing. Also no communication from the devs.

A moderately fun campaign that seems to have been scaled back compared to Boneworks to be able to run on a quest natively, the levels contain smaller set pieces overall and don't give off the same liminal vibe that Boneworks does. Aside from that, the game plays more like a 2h campaign followed by a collection of tech demos that show off cool-ish mechanics that the devs added to this title that weren't in Boneworks. Would be fine if it was like 20 bucks, but at a 40€ price tag I expected a LOT more. It's more expensive than it's predecessor while having LESS content ffs.

The gunplay is slightly improved but also feels lacking in certain areas (HK slapping is extremely inconsistent for some reason, you cannot slap the bolt release in the M4, etc). There is also a distinct lack of different hand poses when holding the gun (lack of a C clamp position, for example) and mag poses (Not having the choice to grab either from the bottom or from the side). Aiming with bigger weapons can be tricky since SLZ insists that guns must collide with your avatar's body, meaning that you have to put the virtual stock of your virtual gun against your janky physics-based virtual body, which more often than not makes the gun tilt to the sides due to goofy collisions. 
You can press grab by the magwell to pull out the current mag on your pistol (which makes no sense since you already have an eject mag button), the issue is that you'll end up pulling your mag out when trying to 2-hand your pistol from the bottom (where you would usually place your palm irl). Shotguns only fire slugs for some god forsaken reason which would be fine if we had the option to load buckshot, but no, only slugs here. Kinda defeats the point of using a shotty in most scenarios since a good rifle headshot tends to kill most things from long range. At the end of the day it's still one of the most satisfying aspects of the game nonetheless, but I expected more improvements when compared to their previous title.

Melee combat is, simply put, abysmal. It seems that the recent patch made it even worse which I find impressive since SLZ never really nailed melee combat. Your character almost always holds the weapon like a complete lobotomite (I can't count the amount of times I unholstered a hammer just to be holding it sideways) which you have to correct manually. Swinging the weapon is another, even sadder story; Your avatar cannot swing a sword normally, period. I don't even know how to explain what he does with the sword, but I sure as hell wouldn't call it a swing. Slashing as a whole simply doesn't exist, you bump your blade against the enemy and sometimes a "damage spot" appears on them like you just hit them with a blunt weapon, stabbing feels good enough though.

The avatar system is interesting but it's clearly meant as a modders ressource more than a proprer game feature, by the time you have all the 6 avatars the game is almost over. The amount of avatars available could also be better (variations of the avatars would be cool, why only have 1 strong, 1 light etc?)

Enemy variety is a real issue to me, you'll see a huge amount of recycled enemies from Boneworks, and not enough interesting new additions. One gripe that I have is that all the human enemies only fistfight you, even the guards in the street puncher level dont attempt to grab an object to hit you with. The only enemy that can shoot you at all in this game (not counting the turret since it's more of an object rather than an enemy) is the omni projector, which is literally just a rolling tripod with a gun that isn't satisfying to shoot. Skeletons are basically nullbodies with a new coat of paint, villagers are all bald for some reason and behave like a ford with altered voicelines, etc. There really isn't anything new here which is a shame.

The story is kinda vague and seems to be there just to set up their next mainline game, but that's alright since the story of Boneworks never really made much sense to me in the first place.

Climbing is still pure jank.

The holsters are still janky.

Hand to hand combat is weird, as blocking doesn't really do much as you still take damage, and since the new patch you can only really use jabs against most enemies since hooks dont seem to be registering as attacks.

I will aknowledge that this game was build more as a modders ressource, a VR Gmod of sorts, rather than a proper mainline game, but the near abandonment this game suffered from by SLZ killed any momentum the game could have had, the modding community is basically dead, you have some weapon packs, NPC reskins and some low quality maps made by children but that's it. I expected to be able to make up for the lack of content in the main game with mods but no, there really isn't anything to do after the game is done. Unless you want to collect every item in the game.

And yeah, item collection is back from Boneworks, albeit with improvements (you dont have to carry the capsules to the end of the level anymore). My problem with this system is that they put EVERY MOTHER-FUCKING PROP IN THE GAME in those capsules, meaning that 95% of the stuff you find is boring. I opened a secret room after backtracking from the office area with a developer keycard, only to find FUCKING [b] TRASH BAG B [/b] inside. Yes, a variant of a trash bag inside a secret room. I just installed a full save after that because there's no way I'm running through the whole game again to get a variant of a park bench.

The soundtrack is an absolute banger though, just like in Boneworks. The karting section for example, which is painfully short and boring on it's own, is made 10x better by the pseudo-eurobeat that plays when you start racing (against no one lmao). Basically, they cooked with the soundtrack, no complaints here.

Stress Level Zero, for the love of god, give this game some love, add some content, interact with your community and try to revitalize interest in this game. Buying the game right now feels like stepping on a sinking ship that never really left the harbour in the first place. There's no real post story content, and there doesn't seem to be anything approaching on the horizon either.

TL:DR Interesting game, way too many reused assets without enough new additions to balance it out, not enough improvements, short story, not enough content overall, great soundtrack, and not worth 40€.

Get it on a sale at best, but curb your expectations (and pray that older mods get updated soon if you're hoping to get more than 6h of playtime).

BONEWORKS was one of the (if not THE) greatest VR games of all time. With how much I enjoyed the first game, and the clear passion that the developers had for IT, I was REALLY excited to see what happened with BONELAB after it was announced.
Let me say it again so it's clear; I LOVED BONEWORKS; this is not me hating both games.

It's BECAUSE I loved BONEWORKS as much as I did that this review hurts all the more.

Tdlr: BONELAB is a buggy mess with absolutely ZERO new ideas to separate it from it predecessor. 

While BONELAB technically does have "new" NPCs and Weapons, they're just either more machine guns, or buggy impact-free shotguns that simply aren't fun to handle.
NPC's are just reskinned Nullmen or Turrets. 

Half of the fun of the original BONEWORKS game was discovering this brand new world you were in, and trying to decipher what the goal of the protagonist actually was!
That's simply not present in BONELAB. You already know what this world is. You as a protagonist simply don't HAVE a goal. 
The new body-swap mechanic (on top of being buggy and broken as hell AND only being unlocked within the LAST HOUR of the game) isn't enough to make players feel like they're experiencing something new at all! It's just VR at different heights, something that VRChat, Chillout, and any VR game with custom characters has been doing for years.

There are two required driving sequences that are either a complete waste of time, being basically a mediocre roller coaster showcase you would have expected to see when VR was first commercially viable; or so ridiculously hard to control that you'll spend more time trying to reorient yourself and your stomach than you will actually driving.

It's clear that the developers had ideas and drive for BONELAB, but clearly not enough to warrant a "full" sequel, and especially not one that COSTS MORE THAN THE FIRST GAME.

Initially, people complained about the first game BONEWORKS; thinking that it was mainly just a tech demo. Obviously, this was wrong; as BONEWORKS actually contained an interesting story, new ideas/characters/USES FOR VR/PERSPECTIVE.
The same argument simply CANNOT be made for BONELAB. It's just BONEWORKS without a story, without new ideas, without interesting use of VR as a medium. BONELAB IS a tech demo of SLZ's new Marrow Engine capabilities. That's not enough for players.

If the game was around $20-25 CAD, I'd feel a little better about it. But, it's $45, which is more than BONEWORKS; and too much for how little there is.

I expected so much better from this game; and it simply couldn't deliver.

The game adds shotguns and other cool weapons! The new weapons feel amazing and the suppressed pistol is my favorite out of them all. The bad:

The first level is pretty good after completing it you are thrown into the bonelab hub, if you want to continue with the story you have to do a crane puzzle which is so glitchy and is not fun after that you reach level 4. You go into a mine and sit in a roller coaster that is pretty enjoyable but what makes it kinda pointless is the fact you can leave your headset somewhere if you entered the cart and just wait for the level to end. Then you have level 6 - 11 you get avatars in those levels, the 6th level is probably the best one and levels 7 9 and of course 11 are the worst levels i played coming from SLZ. 12 Level is pointless and 13th is the best one.

Level Design
Alright in this section im gonna compare the design to the boneworks levels. So first off bonelab's level design feels more linear and it feels like you have less ways to play the levels  in boneworks it felt more open every level felt like a sandbox in bonelab it feels like you are going straight from a to b. There is less stuff to play with less detail and it feels empty. Boneworks is much more open because of the bonelab having to release on quest 2 so they had to optimize the game to work on quest 2. Now for the worst the pillar climb holy ####### shit it really sucks, it is worse level in any game that i have played. Not to mention the moon level which everyone justifies with the point that a map is on spawn but if a lot of people missed it, it means that its not players fault its just bad level design.

The Avatars
The avatars are amazing they are the best thing that has come out of this game. I do have some complaints about the light avatar (Anime maid) being totally useless and the short avatar being used one time in the span of the game.

The advertising 
This game is presented as a boneworks sequel with improved physics but its not the climbing is awful it is also shown like it is a game focused on the story it took me 5 hours to beat this game if the game would be advertised as a gmod with some fun additions i would have no complaints. Also the gameplay trailer shows you a lot of parts of the level ascent which is almost 70% of the level . I came into this game expecting the story to go like this: you enter the bonelab at level 2 then you enter the third level and you get all of the avatars. You continue the story with all those fun avatars like in ascent the problem is in the trailer it looks like those are different levels and there is a lot of content revolved around those avatars guess what you go through ascent then you go to the next level which is the last level in the game. This game feels worse than bonelab, and I believe thats because the arms can collide with things now, not just the hands like in boneworks.  This "campaign" is purely just a tech demo for what the engine can do. And so after finishing it I hoped that maybe mods could bring some life into the game. This is one of those circumstances where I wish I could leave a neutral review. SLZ tried some interesting things with this game and some of them landed, some of them didn't. Don't get me wrong, I really appreciate it when a dev team tries to do interesting things with VR games and commend them for having the guts to do so. The avatar system adds a fun new layer to the combat and puzzles, vehicles are something of a rarity in VR games, there are no other games out as heavily physics based as Bonelab save for its predecessor, and not too terribly many are trying to capture the ease of modding and general gameplay feel of the venerable Gmod. All systems that are on the conceptual level great ideas and often enjoyable. The execution however can be hit and miss, requiring refinement.

On model inventory interaction points (mag pouches and holsters) do not appear to scale properly depending on avatar size and proportion leading to clumsy and inconsistent manipulation depending on what you're playing as (for large avatars they're often too small to interact with easily, for small avatars they're sometimes so large they get in the way of each other's interaction areas). Aside from this, it's very evident that all the equipment in the game was intended for a narrower range of avatar sizes than are present in the base game (larger sized avatars have trouble manipulating most firearms or existing vehicles in game). I wouldn't mind this so much if there were more weapon and vehicle size variety to match the base game avatars. On the topic of vehicles, they are realistic perhaps to a fault in their handling and at times a bit buggy. I'll concede that this might just be a practice problem, but using the steering wheel on most vehicles feels clumsy and imprecise. An option to use joystick based steering would be welcome as would some physics interaction refinement. When I first played the game shortly after launch and reached the roller coaster section sitting in the cart to start the ride resulted in getting stuck clipping into the seat and jittering violently the whole ride. This made use of the mounted gun impossible and resulted in a lot of motion sickness that I don't believe I would have experienced otherwise. On the topic of in game physics, I don't know why but it feels much less polished than in Boneworks. Clipping feels more common, at times the track ball all avatars ride around on for locomotion gets stuck on ledges I'm attempting to mantle and insists on dragging me into certain death despite fully crouching to clear the ledges, and melee still feels kind of clumsy and "sticky" for lack of a better term with bladed objects often getting stuck or not slicing as they should. Lastly there's the sandbox nature of the game. When I think back on what made Garry's Mod fun for me quite a few things come to mind, some which Bonelab captured perfectly and others it lacks. Messing around with props, npcs, and weapons in sandbox maps, that's there. Using available tools to set up my own games with their own objectives for my amusement, that's there too, but I would request that dev tools are available to be spawned anywhere from your interaction menu in NG+. The ability to modify the game with your own systems and mechanics outside the scope of what exists already (weapon customization, custom game modes like prop hunt or spacebuild, additional construction tools, control bindings, etc) is not present yet but is doubtlessly coming as the modding scene for the game grows. The option to enjoy the absurdities with friends in a multiplayer lobby; the absence of this kind of stings. I understand that the incorporation of functional multiplayer into a game is a tall order, a very difficult undertaking, but to take a sandbox game from great to excellent I view it as a requirement.

All in all the effort and care put into this game is self evident, and I believe it to be capable of being excellent, but it's still got a ways to go.

I'll be honest. I wasn't enthused when I first tried bonelab. It wasn't really the game I was expecting. Coming off of boneworks, which I loved and am willing to admit had quite a few issues, I found a lot of problems with bonelab. 

For one, I regocnise that the whole game's purpose was for it to be a modding sandbox. Has it lived up to that? I don't know. I never got mods working. I tried many websites, launchers, guides, the whole nine yards. It just never worked (I'm on PC for reference). The campaign was alright, but not too enthralling and a bit immersion breaking. 

Secondly, the cool environment and aesthetics that boneworks had (and I loved) wasn't present within bonelab. It made sense, yea. You get a new character to unlock and the environment thematically matched that character. That's fine. But, it felt like it switched way too fast too often. Furthermore, there were only two characters that I personally liked, and only one that I used (these being the big strong guy who looks straight outta dark souls and the slim fast girl in the body tight suit (I used the girl mainly cuz she was the only one who was close to matching my body irl)). 

And lastly, and this is a personal gripe of mine (take it with a grain of salt), I never liked how boneworks or bonelabs did full body. I just didn't enjoy it. It's probably the most immersion breaking part of either game. None of the movements feel like something I instigated. If I had to describe it, it feels like riding a segway made of jello. They got in the way of my actions (I.E. making two handing rifles almost impossible), got caught on terain and props that I didn't notice (causing a slight out of body experience as I try to figure out why the character isn't doing what I thought/wanted), and not really tied to what I imagine I'm doing (no, I don't think my foot should be ontop of the box that I just wanted to pick up). If they added an option for full body tracking (which I have and would love to use), then I'm sure a lot of the aforementioned issues would be more/less solved. And, no doubt, there's a mod to fix them. But again, I couldn't get mods working.

Was it fun? Yes. I enjoyed it a bit.

Would I recommend it? No. There were too many bugs when I played it (2 majorly game breaking ones that had me frustrated for hours), and I'd say there are better games for cheaper. 

Overall, I'm disappointed but always willing to give it a second chance. It's a sandbox after all. I'm sure that (if I ever get mods working) I'll find my niche within it given enough time.

BONELAB is one of the single worst VR experiences I've ever had the displeasure of suffering through. It is a step back from BONEWORKS in every way, shape, and form imaginable. BONEWORKS had problems, but despite its numerous issues, it was a well-designed and enjoyable campaign experience with a neat sandbox to go along with it. BONELAB barely has a campaign - what's there is maybe one or two hours long, everything else is sandbox content.
The campaign itself is a confusing mess of uninspired levels meant to introduce the poorly implemented avatar switching system. One of them was literally just a walking sim that forced you to use a tiny avatar with stubby legs to trudge across a lunar landscape - except you can complete the level within two minutes by stepping on two jump pads and pressing a button. The level that follows is a kart racer - which forces you to use an avatar who's too weak to use the tiny steering wheel with one hand, and on top of that, the kart spins out constantly if you apply too much steering angle - which seems to be any more than five degrees in either direction. The "heavy" avatar, which should enable a fun strength power fantasy, is instead a chore to use, since the avatar's hands don't match up with the position of your IRL hands, totally ruining any muscle memory or immersion you may have had.
The climbing physics are also godawful - there's no way to force yourself up and over a ledge, you instead have to mash yourself against it and pray the game lets you on top of it. Furthermore, a majority of avatars are too weak to actually lift themselves up onto an object, adding to the needless irritation.
Movement is floaty and awkward at times. Jumping is awkward most of the time. Climbing is, as mentioned, awful.
Melee combat lacks any and all impact. When I wind up and deliver a huge punch to an enemy while using the "heavy" avatar, I expect the blow to knock him flat on his back, if not fold him like tissue paper or even send him flying. Instead, they just kind of stumble and fall over.
Gunplay is... It's alright. Pretty hard to screw that up, but given how poor of a showing Stress Level Zero put out here, I wouldn't be surprised.

If you want to shoot things, play H3VR
If you want to use melee, play Blade and Sorcery
If you want a moddable sandbox, play BONEWORKS

BONELAB is a failure of a video game and Stress Level Zero should be ashamed of themselves for ever producing it.

This was one of two or three games I actually expected to be good this year. Felt like Boneworks DLC. I held off on writing a review but since finishing it on my second session I have not once felt the "urge" to come back to it.

Shorter, more linear and less interesting campaign. Zero innovation besides the 'avatar switching' with 3 of the 6 avatars being completely redundant ("Strong", Light and Short). It's not a bad game, but I don't know if it's worth recommending if you've played Boneworks. When I saw the medieval setting teased in the intro I just wanted to go and play whatever game THAT was, not what I ended up slogging through for ~6 hours. You end up returning to that area later on but it's a LOT smaller and all the enemies just use their fists even though there are guns and melee weapons lying around everywhere (also enemies cannot use melee weapons in this game, and there is only one enemy type that can use guns; the same copy+pasted hologram enemy from Boneworks).

No new guns except a pump action and semi-auto shotugn, which modders added into Boneworks yonks ago (in fact the devs said they would add shotguns into Boneworks but obviously that never happened). Unless you want to count reskins of course. Good to see the same M4, MP5K etc copy+pasted into this game. On one hand, I want devs to keep content from previous games if the sequel is in the same engine, however I expect to see something NEW when playing a game sold as brand new rather than just picking up the same weapons to kill the same enemies in the same environments.

There are no new enemies except a short, fragile 'turret' type thing which  does a lot of damage but goes down in a couple shots. Only shows up in the last 2(?) levels. They also remodeled/reskinned a couple enemies from the first game. The blue zombie type enemies are not present in the campaign but are in the other modes, so there is very little variety when playing.

You've probably already read stuff about the Moonbase and 'Pillar' levels, though these criticisms pale in comparison to the other issues I feel the game has.

This game's only saving grace is ironically what probably made it such an underwhelming experience; massive marketing (externally and in-game, integrated into the canon story of the game lol) focused on modding and player made content - would've been no problem in my opinion if the initial offering wasn't so sparse and shallow. Hopefully players can add campaigns and new game modes to extend the longevity of the game as it currently does nothing better than its competitors; 

Blade and Sorcery wins melee and stealth, 
Hellsplit and Grimlord win 'dark'/difficult combat, 
H3VR and Contractors win firearms,
Hard bullet wins 'brutal' sandbox gameplay...

...not to mention the janky impact physics and amateur sounds that abound this game. Main draw of this game is structured levels so without that sort of content there is no real draw as long as there are other games with 'endless' modes that feel better to play.

But the worst of all is that the music in this game is somehow worse than Boneworks. Boneworks has one of the best OSTs in gaming, undoubtedly the best of any VR game. The main theme is subtly included in a few tracks here but otherwise the entire soundtrack in Bonelab is forgettable, and for some reason they decided to include strange, almost slurred vocals in one of the songs. Maybe my problem is that I am not a hipster but this was a total L and took me out of the game (the 'game' being walking around the HUB and being forced to try random minigames before being able to continue playing the walking simulator-esque campaign.

Finally, the game is unbelievably easy, almost as easy as Boneworks. The most trouble one would have in this game is climbing, as the legs sometimes go all wack and twist 90 degrees to the side or get stuck in ladder rungs. Maybe it was a few one-offs for me, so in general the climbing and movement was very similar to Boneworks so the muscle memory carried over. Most enemies die in one or two headshots and the enemies are typically few and far between, and you have a Borderlands-style 'last chance' if you die where you can revive yourself by getting a kill. I also detest the ammo system in this game just as I did in Boneworks; you have a total pool of ammo that carries over between levels, and you don't lose ammo in magazines if you throw them away so there is little care for ammo management. This means you use very little ammo in combat and will always be able to top up your mag without worrying about 'wasting' ammo. The weird thing about this is that the system had a use in Boneworks as ammo was a currency used to buy things (like weapons or developer tools) from vending machines, which are completely absent in this game. I wish they went with a different system, perhaps like having an ammo limit or needing to put ammo physically on your body a la H3VR/etc.

Anyway, rant over. While this review was mostly negative, the game is good, but not the revolutionary experience they advertised it as. The whole ending felt very on-the-nose, and there is even a Discord link to a modding server at the end for those looking to get into modding. There is a bit of polish compared to the prequel and they added one or two cool new things but this just seems like a modding platform - a double edged sword that I love and hate. Modded games last longer and the experience of tailoring your mod list is great, but there is a niggling feeling at the back of my head suggesting that developers use this as an excuse to underdevelop their game as players will just fix it later (Bethesda moment). Not sure if SLZ are like that, so far it seems not, but my main takeaway from this game was that it's an okay if underwhelming experience with massive potential for future improvement. Maybe in a year we will see videos titled "Bonelab is GREAT if you don't play the campaign..." or "This mod makes Bonelab worth playing again" or "This epic mod FIXES Bonelab".

The Good:

- Guns rock. This is coming from a guy who almost exclusively plays VR shooters and shoots on the weekends as a hobby. Everything about it feels visceral and punchy in a way that makes the occasional animation related jank easy to overlook, with the exception of a couple guns which stand out as being particularly annoying to use the to the weight simulation.

- When the immersion hits, it HITS. Sure, the settings can be kinda bland at times, but even in those circumstances there are moments that stand out as being really awe inspiring despite how simple they are.

- The soundtrack, for the most part, is top notch. Even though blasting through generic NPCs with a Glock to the sound of synthwave should be played out by now, it most definitely is not. Not in VR, anyways

- The Tac Trials and the Rooftop Parkour minigames are so god damned cool, even if they kind of suck to play

- Driving is generally pretty fun, at least in my opinion. I've got good vr legs and love whipping around in the go-karts :)

The Bad:

Campaign too short, IK sucks. I don't care how cool or immersive it is watching a playermodel's arms move in place of mine while I smash open a crate, or rack the slide on a pistol, or shove a giant ball of trash around if the other half of the time its only purpose seems to be 'get in the way of everything the player wants to do'. 

It's one thing for a game mechanic to be super realistic and well built, and yes, the physics are generally very cool and fun to toy around with, but any sense of immersion or enjoyment of them is often broken by the unfortunate reality of physics engines, in that they all suck in their own special ways, and will break eventually.

That said, you shouldn't have to fight against a game's physics engine, especially in VR, unless it's designed for you to do so in a consistent manner, and consistent physics don't easily mesh with full player bodies unless you have full-body trackers or a lot of patience. It would be one thing if the game was more tuned to allow people to get used to and work around the jank and the artificial weightiness, but unfortunately, a lot of the movement in this game is just way too sluggish for such an important mechanic.

For instance, the game really tries to be a platformer sometimes, there's a whole section dedicated to it in the form of that godawful pillar level everyone hates. The problem is that you can't climb for shit and jumping is quite possibly the most unintuitive part of the game, with it being tied to a button that at first appears to make you crouch and slow down a bit and then has this weird sort of delay before your character's legs even lift off. 

80% of the time, you'll try to climb up, onto, or over something and your characters legs will get stuck, and you'll wind up sliding back down it like a shitty mall cop. I made sure that my height and arm length were set correctly and everything, and I still wound up doing all of, but not limited to the following things;

- getting my own melee weapons tangled in my characters arms somehow

- missing jumps that a toddler could clear with relative ease

- looping my arms through the rungs of ladders

- flinging myself off of obstacles that I was half wrapped around

Not to mention the fact that the right thumbstick, for some reason, controls your in-game stance, which as far as I can tell can't be disabled. As an accessibility feature, it could be nice, and I'll give kudos for that, but it's usefulness is kind of debatable and I'd much rather the controller bind be spent on something more useful

Also, the puzzles are generally difficult to figure out at first, because the game isn't great at explaining, and you can't at all tell when you're getting shot before you start to black out.
