[h1] PART 0: HTC VIVE Support [/h1]

[b] For anyone playing on HTC Vive, you'll want to read this. [/b]

BONELAB does not support Vive wands. The developers have said that themselves, although I only found that out after purchasing.

They do not plan on implementing Vive wand support either as it would be a "waste of time" to include support for a VR headset's native controllers used by [url=https://www.statista.com/statistics/265018/proportion-of-directx-versions-on-the-platform-steam/] 6.21% of all Steam VR users, including Oculus SteamVR users. [/url] This may not sound like much, but that still contains a lot of people.

The way they flat out do not support such a [b] widely known [/b] headset's controllers is crazy to me. There's definitely money to be made with Vive users, but they can't be a**ed to actually implement the proper controller binds for the game. Personally, I feel this is because of personal bias towards the Vive headset. Especially considering that - at least, from what i've heard - BONEWORKS mocks Vive users using the Vive wand controllers.

I also feel it is very poorly communicated that the game does not support Vive wands. I had no idea they were not supported until I went looking for a fix for the many, many easily fixable issues with using the wands.

Now onto issues with the actual game.

[h2] PART 1: The Issues With The Actual Game™️ [/h2]

The game was not advertised as what it really is: a modding sandbox game. This lead people into believing the game is like a sequel to BONEWORKS, only to be disappointed by the mediocre (and very short, like 4.5 hours long short) story portion of the game. The main gimmick of the game, avatars, is only given to the player after the halfway point of the story. This means you barely get to use avatars in an actual playthrough of BONELAB.

You may say, [i] "Oh well, the game is meant to be modded and messed around with anyways." [/i] There are two major problems with this.

[h3] PART 1.1: The Modding Sucks [/h3]

There is no public SDK for the game yet, meaning it is very difficult to mod the game. On top of that, the very few mods that are available for the game get entirely broken after every patch the game has. The lack of content in the game post-Patch 5 is abysmal. Most mods shown in any mod showcase videos are missing entirely, either because they do not work for the current patch or because the mod developer has quit the community and taken their mods down because of past wrongdoings coming to light/the toxic community (generally from Quest users, no offense) begging mod developers to make their mods compatible with Quest even if it is not possible.

[h3] PART 1.2: The Community Sucks Too [/h3]

Speaking of the toxic community, yes, the BONELAB community is incredibly toxic. It is not welcoming whatsoever and I have seen so much sh*t about people being harassed into leaving the community entirely. This is not really SLZ's fault, moreso the fault of undisciplined, unsupervised kids.

[h2] PART 2: Maybe It's Not All Bad [/h2]

I'm not here to entirely sh*t on BONELAB (that's a lie, I pretty much am). The game has some good pros, in contrast of the many, many cons. The gun and physics systems in the game are very satisfying to use and I feel BONELAB sets a new standard for VR games (leaving a LOT of room for improvement).

[h2] PART 3: I Played More Than You Think [/h2]

I only have 3.8 hours on the game as of writing, and only around ~20 minutes of it was actual gameplay. The rest was trying to fix the multiple bugs I found even in the LOADING MENU for f*cks sake. I have a lot more hours on my old Quest 2, which I used before I swapped to Vive. I say this because my low play time may make people reading this think I don't know what I'm talking about.

[h2] PART 4: I Suck At Making Reviews [/h2]

This review may be a bit [i] "unorganized," [/i] in a way. Randomly changing topics about issues with the game and all that. That's mainly because I have a very bad attention span and there's also so much to talk about that no matter what I do I'll never fully cover everything.

[h2] PART 5: Should You Buy It? [/h2]

I have no idea.

I recommend watching both positive and negative reviews of the game on YouTube before buying. That way, you can weigh the pros and cons for yourself with both sides of the story. Personally, I'm refunding this sack of sh*t if Steam will let me.

[h1] A Final Disclaimer [/h1]

There's also a bug with OpenXR which causes some players to not be able to load in the game. This can be fixed by going into your SteamVR settings, turning on advanced settings, and setting your OpenXR runtime (SteamVR>Settings>Show Advanced Settings>OpenXR>Current OpenXR runtime) to whichever decides to finally work. If that doesn't fix it, your next best option would be to pray to god, the holy spirit, allah, or whatever the h*ll you believe in that it randomly starts working for no reason. It randomly decided to work for me after I restarted my PC, but for others it has just decided not to work whatsoever. In that case, I suggest you make a negative review of the game and refund it. Review bombing tends to make developers actually listen.

BoneLab is nothing like this. When I watched the promotional videos and whatnot, I thought it would be a story-driven sequel to BW, with similar writing. That is almost the exact opposite of what actually was released. There were some good parts to the game, but they all occurred in about the first hour of play through. I'll divide up my review to (hopefully) make it more readable.

[h1] The Good of BoneLab [/h1]

-It introduces new weapons that are somewhat interesting
-Introduces native support for modding
-Includes an updated physics engine from BW (more about this later)

[h1] The Bad of BoneLab [/h1]

-Absolutely horrible story
           This game started strong, but quickly made me want to toss my headset in the trash. As other reviewers have gone into detail, I won't write much here, but suffice it to say, they suck. The minigames that are forced into the campaign ruin the flow of the story and add nothing to the game. The body changing levels simply make no sense other than showing how well the devs can integrate that system into the game. After playing through the rest of the story, I can confidently say that I didn't use this system more than once. Maybe it would have been better if the system wasn't introduced with only about 15% of the story left.

       The story here was nonexistent and seemed to be a bunch of different ideas all compiled and shoved randomly into a cash-grab disguised as a game. 

-Weird physics system
       While BW had a wonky physics engine sometimes, it was undeniably better than BoneLab's most of the time. In BoneLab, half the time you'll go to climb something, or vault a ledge, and you'll find your legs will catapult you in the opposite direction. This causes you to repeat part, or all, of the level. This is especially tough since you cannot do anything about your leg position, when crouching either doesn't work, or makes your virtual head be glued to the floor, making you unable to move. 

-Overly simple level design
       Once again, BW shines much brighter than this game. BW allowed you to explore every nook and cranny to find hidden items and ammo (more on this later). If you wanted to, however, you could progress through BW fairly quickly without the exploring. BoneLab provides almost no exploration, and even when it does, the "hidden" areas provide essentially nothing. One level specifically has you find a "hidden" spot just to find two chairs and writing on the wall. This makes exploring basically useless. Most levels just force your down the story path as it is literally THE ONLY path you can take, with no dead ends or anything to make people curious. This makes even longer levels seem extremely short and underwhelming. 

-Ammunition/guns
       One question: Why make guns and ammo stay through the levels and remove the option to purchase items with ammo? I basically was extremely stringent on shooting enemies because in BW every bullet mattered. You could buy different weapons, and at the end, you could buy dev tools with your saved ammo. BoneLab lets you keep ammo through the levels, and doesn't give you a way to do anything except shoot things  with it. I wound up finishing the game with large amounts of unused ammo. You will get enough ammo to essentially run the whole game doing nothing but shooting enemies. I could have probably avoided 1.5 hours of game play by simply shooting everything and not worrying about how else to kill things. Also guns are perpetually saved as well, so you can keep the guns you initially get throughout the game. Gun spawns later in the game seem to be worse than those in the earlier levels. 
        Also, the final level gives you a ton of guns and lots of ammo to choose from/pick up. I thought from all these items it would be a huge battle like the clock tower in BW. I get to the end of the level and maybe shot 20 bullets to kill 6 enemies. Unlike in BW, where you either had to buy or find weapons to survive tough enemy waves, BoneLab hands you enough guns and ammo to play through the story five times in the first level. (You can also just play as the heavy and kill everything with one punch)

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
       I really wanted to like this game, but it just does not meet even my lowest expectations. If I had known I'd be spending $40 on a compiled list of tech demos and concept ideas, I would not have bought the game. There is almost no story development or reason to continue playing. In BW, even if you didn't understand the story right away, you felt an urge to lay simply to escape the world. Here it just seems like the developers wanted to show off their programming abilities and get a bunch of money from people that simply wanted a playable game. When I first got into the game, as the levels progressed, it felt more and more like a beta or early-access game. If you have BW, do not waste your money on this unfinished cash-grab.

[h1] TLDR [/h1]

[b]On 6th June 2024, Stress Level Zero FINALLY shipped a Bonelab update. If you somehow dig up this review, do note that it was written in August 2023. My criticism towards their approach to the game and lack of communication still stands.[/b]

------------------------------------

Bonelab could have been an amazing sandbox game for VR but its been almost completely let down by the totally moronic approach to its core feature and primary selling point: the modding.

Over the course of development, it seems that Stress Level Zero didn't even bother to reach out to their passionate modding community from Boneworks for feedback and ideas regarding how Bonelab's modding systems should be shaped. Instead of doing the most obvious course of action towards building a game like this, they released Bonelab with a barebones SDK that you can't even create grabbable objects with and a repository based distribution system that was not only replaced by mod.io immediately, but has only ever been used by the community to relay mod.io content to technologically inept Quest 2 users. They also have an approval system to allow modders to contribute to the lore of the game under the guise of canon and non-canon "black market" mods, which is such an awesome concept, and would be even better if they actually approved more than 2 mods and ones that weren't made by themselves.

Then we were promised at least 2 years of updates from the devs. The game hasn't received a non-beta patch since [b]November 2022[/b], the SDK hasn't been updated since [b]October 2022[/b], and since launch we have had ZERO proper communicative updates or dedicated blog posts on any official channels telling us in detail what future plans they have for Bonelab and what they're currently working on, despite an IN-GAME noticeboard stating they would be posting development updates and teases for upcoming additions there. There was even a fully setup [url=https://trello.com/b/XXmsmyEk/bonelab-public]Trello board[/url] you could access in the game from the Mods booth that was removed in patch 1 and left completely unused. 

Now in Stress Level Zero's recluse, this game is being completely carried by the talent in the modding scene. So far they've forked the SDK and have been advancing it on their own; bringing us new gun packs, flying vehicles and polished interactable custom maps. There is also a code mod injector allowing for QOL changes (sometimes [url=https://bonelab.thunderstore.io/package/notnotnotswipez/ForeverMortal/]bringing back stuff from Boneworks[/url] that was oddly downgraded for BL), proper [url=https://bonelab.thunderstore.io/package/notnotnotswipez/ModioModNetworker/]mod.io integration[/url] to allow for a steam workshop-like experience for obtaining mods and an incredible fully functioning [url=https://bonelab.thunderstore.io/package/Lakatrazz/Fusion/]multiplayer mod[/url] with its own tools for custom gamemodes and cosmetics.

If I were SLZ, I would have put Bonelab into early access. Look at how well Warpfrog have done with Blade & Sorcery, they have spent almost FIVE years not only perfecting their game mechanic and content-wise for 1.0, but also taking appropriate feedback from the community to dish up some extraordinary modding tools, bringing together probably the most refined VR murder sim sandbox on the market topped off with an in-game mod manager to allow people to easily obtain mods and intricate development updates published frequently by their community lead. The shining example was right there the whole entire time, and SLZ have never bothered to take a single page from that book.

I'm honestly so confused as to what went wrong and why they're still doing it wrong despite community outcry and the game slowly but visibly fizzling out. These developers are proven to be highly talented and would even act rather promptly on user feedback during updates for Boneworks. Why on earth has their approach to a sandbox focused game built by user feedback and content from modders been so braindead and void of any actual community engagement?! Where is the communication? Where is the roadmap? Where are the damn updates we were promised? 

I really do love Bonelab, even in its current state. Its actually a very worthy successor for Boneworks; refining the feel of physical interactions a lot, introducing an incredible avatar system and the mods are still brilliant despite the lack of official support. But the vague, unfulfilled promises and lack of communication this far into the games determined lifespan are a huge show of dishonesty from Stress Level Zero and overall an utter f*cking joke. According to the Patch #2 changelog blog post, the team reads all of these reviews and our feedback is very helpful! 

So here is my helpful feedback for SLZ:

In a vacuum I would recommend Bonelab without hesitation. But Bonelab was not released into a vacuum, it has to prove itself against the overwhelming expectations that came with the popularity of its predecessor. 

While Bonelab offers a similar structure as Boneworks, the focus was shifted away from the campaign towards mini-games and time trials. The campaign is not only much shorter than Boneworks', it is also much smaller in scale and strictly linear. You will mainly traverse narrow corridors with no side areas to explore. The overwhelming sense of scale Boneworks was delivering is completely lost in Bonelab. 

As compensation you get more short game modes like the tac trials, arena modes and parkour challenges, all of which have leaderboards you can fight your way up on. For me personally, that is not a good exchange. I loved Boneworks for its very intense set piece moments, that pushed the capabilities of the VR medium to their absolute limits. You find these only in the campaign. 

From a technical standpoint Bonelab offers a very similar experience as Boneworks did. The physics based interaction engine Stress Level Zero created for Boneworks still manages to impress but was not extended or built upon. The only new addition is a custom avatar system which is pulled straight out of a VR social app and feels very out of place in a single-player only game. 

Bonelab encourages the players to create themselves but without offering in-game creation tools. If you want to contribute as a modder you will need to know at least some Unity basics. It is possible that the game will manage to cultivate an active modding scene to add the content it so sorely needs. If this happens the value could increase significantly in the future. 

It feels wrong to not recommend Bonelab, but it would feel disingenuous to recommend it. A binary rating system falls short here. The best thing I could come up with is to describe why I felt disappointed by Bonelab. If you resonate with the things I wrote in this review, chances are you will be disappointed too. To end this on a good note: The Soundtrack fucking slaps!

Sloplab. For a game that is constantly priced higher than its predecessor and most VR games, it really lacks quality. In the base game you get "13" levels, 8 being filler levels. By the time you finish all the filler levels, the game gives you one good level, a "story" level then the game ends. Hell, I remember being audibly confused when I first finished the game due to how short the campaign was. The rest of the non filler levels are very simple in design compared to the "approach every situation how you want to" design that the previous game BOASTED about in its tutorial. This design made the game easy. To explain how easy the game is, the AI is incredibly brain dead. The melee enemies constantly fall over, causing them perform their 30s stand up animation, making them unsatisfying to kill. Additionally, the game gives you guns way too often. In the previous game, at the end of each level there was a field that would delete all your weapons. This would make the game more challenging for you as you had to get creative on how to defend yourself in every level, since you couldn't rely on your previous collection of guns. In Bonelab they save your weapons from level to level, meaning you can save your overpowered weapons to each level and kill everything without a challenge. Finally the avatar system ALSO MAKES THE GAME EASY. If you avatar is slightly strong, then all of your guns will basically have no recoil. If you have an avatar that is somewhat obese then you will basically not die. If you have an avatar who is tall you can basically skip most of the level. Some people may think that this is a creative way of solving the level, but I think its a boring way to cheese through the campaign. 

"But what about the sandbox and mods" if you a good sandbox and mod experience in VR buy Gmod and install the VR mod. What Gmod has did in 2006 is EXTREMELY better than what this game has done with its sandbox and mods. To name a few example, Gmod has a better objects menu, more tools, better tools (ex:making welds invisible), the ability to save your scene, a PROPER PHYSICS GUN, ragdolls (you don't need to kill NPC), a lower barrier to entry, base game multiplayer, better base game campaign (Half-Life 2) and this is for the user side. I am personally not a moder, but what I've SEEN, the SDK that Gmod has allows for more creativity and complexity for mod makers. If you want a quality VR game, please consider other games, If you want a VR sandbox, PLEASE consider Gmod with the VR mod installed.

This really could have been a positive review, with me having little to no bad things to say about it. I'm guessing few people, if anyone will read this review as Bonelab's launch has come and gone, but I'll go ahead. Us players playing bonelab were met with assets carried over from other SLZ games, and unfinished half-assed campaign with bad empty levels that were either comically easy, or frustratingly hard- not hard due to difficulty, but due to terrible level design or it taking far too long. For example, Short. Short has absolutely no upsides, and the only time you would voluntarily choose him over other characters is during sections going through small spaces. If I only ever pick a character because I'm forced to, that's bad game design. However, the biggest issue with short was not the character, but his awful level. Short doesn't have a minigame level like other character's do, but instead a sandbox level on the moon with low gravity. Short has legs that are, you guessed it, short and stubby. Because of this he can't run very fast, and what is the gameplay of the moon level? Walking. A LOT of walking. So what breaks up the walking, puzzle or enemies to fight? Nothing at all. However, much of the walking I did was just random wandering because there is a map in the spawn area I had no idea about. Why did I just walk past without noticing? The map is poorly lit and not drawn much attention to, and all previous character introductory levels had no such thing. So I walked past without a care. This would already make a horrendous experience, but just to add a bit of icing on the cake, there was an item spawner right outside the spawn where I could make any item I wanted. Including ammo. Needless to say, I didn't care about ammo for the short rest of the game. Although Short is no doubt the worst offender, every level has some low quality aspect like this. Missing textures, weak and unchallenging enemies, sparsely detailed areas, things such as this ruin the game. However, it is very clearly built for modding, so what about that? I won't deny the modding scene is amazing, with passionate modders making game-changing mods everywhere. But the mod integration in game... just doesn't work. Blade and Sorcery, a game not even built specifically for modding, can do this just fine. Okay, but even with all of this, the game is having constant updates fixing the game-breaking jank and adding more content... right? No. The most recent update was in 2022, and with no community updates so far here is no sign of any more updates or more content. Will I continue to play bonelab? Probably so. Despite this, I can't reccomend it to anybody else. Especially coming from boneworks, you will be disappointed like I and most everybody else was. If you want to play a good vr shooter, try Vertigo 2.

UPDATE: Patches
To start, I should note that Short's level has been fixed! Sorta. The map is better lit, and there is a large beacon showing you exactly where to go. Plus, there little boosters than make you fly through the air. But because you know where everything is and exactly what to do with nothing inbetween, the whole level takes about 1 minute. It's just a minor time waste and does a bad job of representing what Short will mostly be doing, climbing through small holes. However, moving on, Patch 4 released. It came out on June 6, 2024. The patch before it came out in November 20, 2022. You can probably see the problem. The patch provided quality of life things, and extra stuff for modders. Also, proper modding integration! Finally, it only took THAT long after release to correctly do the very thing it was built for. Now, the campaign. In the patch, there were minor things that directly affected it. But, it's still bad. MINOR SPOILERS (but you'll get to it in less than 5 hours anyways): In the end taxi, you are told about some sort of mysterious enemy that you have to combat by "creating". The campaign is over, and all that's left is the little postgame content and mods. The enemies in the last game were quite flawed, they weren't able to go up inclines, or use weapons, except for the one enemy that could, which didn't really have a physics body. Although, the game was still fun. The problem with Bonelab is that it's just the same game but worse.

The maps in Boneworks were large, complex and cool, with unique enemy encounters that were actually interesting and fun. Different sections provided different moods, like the sewer area, being spooky and dark, or the tower, full of interactable objects and enemies. In bonelab the maps were nowhere near as good, basically always just being a room. Or a less detailed open space area. I think this might be because of the limitations of being on Quest.

Although, Bonelab isn't really such a bad experience, the main problem is the fact that the campaign is way too short to be so expensive, especially with so many flaws. The game is just trying to rely on user-generated content, which is really bad for a 39.99$ game.

In conclusion, Bonelab has a short, mediocre campaign with maps that are limited. It has virtually no improvement on gameplay to Boneworks and is just a quest port of Boneworks' physics engine.
Although, I am not saying that you shouldn't buy it, the user-generated content is probably quite good, though it is very disappointing that the last game had such a good campaign, and how Bonelab failed to improve on the mechanics of Boneworks and have an equally good campaign.

TLDR: Bonelab is not a very good improvement on Boneworks, having a worse and shorter campaign. It lacks any actual improvements on the mechanics of Boneworks and fails to address its shortcomings. Though, it can still be a fun game for those who could enjoy its user-generated content.

Edit: it could be worth buying also because of the fact that there is a mod porting the boneworks campaign to it, although I cannot comment on its quality as I have not played that mod. So, I am not sure whether the mod could capture the full experience of Boneworks.

First off, I want to say: I really, really wanted to like this game. Boneworks, as is known, was a huge leap forward for VR when it first released, and I still think that statement holds up today. It really felt like the first fully-realized VR shooter of full quality. A lot of that was due to how robust the campaign mode was; at first, the game felt like an experimental tech demo leaning on its fourth wall, but later on, you realize how much more the game has to offer. It was slow to reveal the full extent of its hand, and that really worked in its favor.
I mention this because Bonelabs is its opposite, in that way. It starts strong, interesting, intriguing - and then slowly but surely it becomes a glorified tech demo, but for real this time. And that's really sad to me, because it really seems like it should be the other way around. Boneworks, for all of its strong points, was still a highly experimental game that had areas in need of refinement. Climbing ledges occasionally proved impossible, ladders were painful, and the game generally hinged far too much on climbing that didn't feel all that great and left you at constant risk of falling and losing progress. Bonelabs, instead of trying to improve the physics of these interactions, just makes it so you barely have to do them at all. This was a perfect chance to refine the game to make interactions smoother, and they just... aren't. Janky as it was, and the addition of new bodytypes can actually exaggerate the problem. Bonelabs also feels very tech-demo in the sense that there's no real progression; you can find some of the better weapons in the game early on, and since all carried items stay on between loads, you can go through the entire game with the exact same set of weapons. Hell, later levels seem to have actively worse weapons, somehow. The usage of ammo as currency has also been completely removed, which makes it so you're never at any sort of scarcity or need to conserve. If you're not spraying every single room you enter three times over with machine pistols, you're never going to run out of anything. There is even a level in the [i]base campaign[/i] that has Sandbox mode's build gun directly in front of you when you start, which means that you can generate quite literally infinite ammo. Why even have limited ammo as a concept if it's barely used? This also makes it so that exploration feels a lot cheaper. There's precious few places where you're rewarded for finding a secret in a way that actually gives you something cool. There's not much TO explore, really, most of the campaign is completely linear. The only real thing you get as exploration rewards are capsules that let you have some toys in Sandbox mode, and I really could not care less about them.
That sums up a lot of the game, actually. The single player feels like it's just tacked on to a sandbox game. The game's new mechanic - switching bodies - is only put into the player's control at the very end of the game, and it's barely even needed there. The story of the first game was a little hard to work out, but it was interesting, and would've been perfect to explore further; and now, the story is barely even in the room, with a fuzzy non-ending that comes too soon and says nothing. The whole game just feels half-baked, which is just confusing, as it seems like there was so much to build off of. I wouldn't say I hated this game, I just desperately wish it could've been better.
(Edit! I've gotten into modding, which seems to be what SLZ was banking on with this game. MarrowSDK needs about double the amount of documentation that it has right now, and that's after 6 patches that also broke a lot of mods in the process. While we're at it, why did SLZ go through the effort to put in butt softbody physics, but not to put in any sort of third-person spectator camera? Why put in a feature that no one can even see, and why is that feature my cheeks? Aside from that, there's been minor tweaks to the main campaign to add some secrets, and ammo economy actually matters now that it's sort of a scoring system, but it still doesn't help the campaign's actual pacing.)

Rewriting this review to account for the game having been out for over a year and a half. Bonelab plays well but is a skeleton of a game. It's meant to be seen as a template for mods but the mod tools still aren't even finished yet. Yes, it can be modded currently but they're all either broken/janky/bad with a few exceptions. The Labworks mod to import the campaign from Boneworks is a must have and feels like it should've been included with the game on launch as an unlockable. Bonelab alone should not cost more than Boneworks in the state that it is in. Wait for the update to properly finish what this game was built for and buy it on sale under $20.

If you are just getting the game for the campaign (which is what I got it for) then you might want to skip out on this. The campaign has like 4 levels that are actually story and the rest are just pointless mini games that give you some avatars that aren't really required to beat the game, as you could beat the entire game as fast or strong. (there are 6 in total, 3 of them are pointless)

 The modding is really the only reason to buy the game, as it is pretty good and the community has made some very cool and impressive mods, but even the modding has its flaws. It's super annoying to set up, and the modding sdk isn't even finished after almost a year. (IT ONLY GOT UPDATED ONE TIME IN OCTOBER JUST A MONTH AFTER THE GAME CAME OUT LMAO) The in game mod manager is completely unusable, and not nearly as easy as advertised, but the modding community has your back instead of the devs!

Boneworks had a much better campaign. This game is very short too. It does have a ton of community generated content, but the game uses it as a crutch instead of having an actual campaign. The avatar mechanic is cool, and amazing from a technical perspective. A Boneworks-like game (well I guess this is a Boneworks sequel) is a great thing to have on the Quest 2. Since there's not a ton of other options for a game like this on the Quest, many problems can be forgiven. This review is for the PCVR version though, and on PCVR there's another better option: Boneworks.
          (If you wanted to you can play through a community port of the Boneworks campaign in Bonelab. Which means you'll be able to play Boneworks with an updated engine, but c'mon that's basically still Boneworks.)
